1

NestJS fundamentals: provider, controller, module, bootstrap

The goal of this section is to make NestJS feel concrete. There are four moving pieces and each one has a distinct job.

ProviderContains reusable application logic and is managed by Nest with @Injectable().
ControllerMaps HTTP requests to methods and delegates the real work to providers.
ModuleExplicitly lists controllers and providers so Nest can wire them together.
BootstrapStarts the app with NestFactory.create(AppModule) and begins listening.

Provider

@Injectable() means Nest is allowed to create and manage this class. It is the NestJS equivalent of a Spring @Service or @Component.

verification.service.ts 
// Given, unchanged - the exact provider from the demo.
import { Injectable } from "@nestjs/common";

@Injectable()
export class VerificationService {
  private readonly knownUsers = ["dave", "erin", "frank"];

  verify(username: string): boolean {
    return this.knownUsers.includes(username);
  }
}

Controller

The controller is the HTTP front door. Constructor injection gives it the already-created service instance; the controller never calls new VerificationService().

verification.controller.ts 
// Given, unchanged - the exact controller from the demo.
import { Controller, Get, Param } from "@nestjs/common";
import { VerificationService } from "./verification.service";

@Controller("verify")
export class VerificationController {
  constructor(private readonly verificationService: VerificationService) {}

  @Get(":username")
  checkUsername(@Param("username") username: string) {
    const verified = this.verificationService.verify(username);
    return { username, verified };
  }
}

Module wiring

Nest modules are explicit. If a controller or provider is omitted from the module metadata, Nest will not wire it automatically.

app.module.ts - starter 
import { Module } from "@nestjs/common";
import { VerificationController } from "./verification.controller";
import { VerificationService } from "./verification.service";
import { AttemptsController } from "./attempts.controller";
import { AttemptsService } from "./attempts.service";

// TODO 2: add AttemptsController to the controllers array, and
// AttemptsService to the providers array, alongside the Verification
// pieces already here. Without this, injecting AttemptsService into
// AttemptsController fails, even though both classes are written
// correctly.
@Module({
  controllers: [VerificationController],
  providers: [VerificationService],
})
export class AppModule {}

After the lab wiring change:

app.module.ts - completed 
@Module({
  controllers: [
    VerificationController,
    AttemptsController
  ],
  providers: [
    VerificationService,
    AttemptsService
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

Bootstrap

reflect-metadata matters because Nest dependency injection reads runtime type metadata from constructor parameters.

main.ts 
import "reflect-metadata";
import { NestFactory } from "@nestjs/core";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log("Listening on http://localhost:3000");
}

bootstrap();
Two phases: at startup Nest builds the dependency graph once. During requests, the controller simply calls methods on the provider instance it already has.
tsx gotcha: the course specifically demonstrates that tsx can silently break Nest dependency injection because its esbuild pipeline does not emit the decorator metadata Nest expects. Use the real tsc build for these labs.
Quiz hint

Be able to explain why a route can be missing entirely when the controller is not registered, versus throwing a dependency error when the controller exists but its provider is missing.

Wire the ranch before you work the ranch. If the module does not know about a controller or provider, nothing downstream can save the request.
2

DTOs and validation: runtime trust boundaries

TypeScript can protect the code you write. It cannot validate arbitrary JSON sent by a client. DTOs and ValidationPipe close that gap.

DTO

A DTO is a class describing the shape of a request body. Its decorators define what values are acceptable at runtime.

Validation decorators

@IsString(), @IsNotEmpty(), @MinLength(), and @IsEmail() enforce rules before the route handler executes.

Global ValidationPipe

A single global pipe can apply validation to all routes. That avoids repeating validation setup on every controller method.

Register DTO

register.dto.ts 
import {
  IsEmail,
  IsNotEmpty,
  IsString,
  MinLength
} from "class-validator";

export class RegisterDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MinLength(3)
  username!: string;

  @IsString()
  @MinLength(8)
  password!: string;

  @IsString()
  @IsEmail()
  email!: string;
}

Global pipe

main.ts 
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    whitelist: true,
    forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
  }),
);

whitelist: true strips fields not declared by the DTO. forbidNonWhitelisted: true goes further and rejects the entire request.

Why unknown fields matter: a registration request containing an undeclared field like isAdmin: true should not be quietly accepted. Rejecting it is a security control, not just API neatness.

Missing field

A missing required property can produce several validation messages at once. The controller body never runs.

Wrong type

A numeric username is rejected at runtime even though TypeScript cannot type-check JSON arriving over HTTP.

Unexpected property

With forbidNonWhitelisted, undeclared fields cause a 400 response instead of being silently carried forward.

Quiz hint

Expect the distinction between a TypeScript interface and a DTO: one is a compile-time shape, the other is a runtime validation boundary.

3

Auth service skeleton: prove the contract before hardening it

This module intentionally keeps two pieces insecure for one stage: plain-text passwords and stub token strings. The endpoint contract is proven first.

RegisterCreate a user, reject duplicates with 409 Conflict.
LoginCheck credentials, reject failures with 401 Unauthorized.
RefreshAccept a valid refresh token and issue a fresh access token.
Logout labInvalidate the stored refresh token so it cannot be reused.
auth.service.ts - skeleton 
private readonly users = new Map<string, StoredUser>([
  ["alice", {
    password: "mission123",
    refreshToken: null
  }],
]);

register(username: string, password: string) {
  if (this.users.has(username)) {
    throw new ConflictException(
      `${username} is already registered`
    );
  }

  this.users.set(username, {
    password,
    refreshToken: null
  });

  return { username, registered: true };
}

login(username: string, password: string) {
  const user = this.users.get(username);

  if (!user || user.password !== password) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      "invalid username or password"
    );
  }

  // issue stub access + refresh tokens
}

refresh(refreshToken: string) {
  const entry = this.findByRefreshToken(refreshToken);

  if (!entry) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      "invalid or expired refresh token"
    );
  }

  const [username] = entry;

  return {
    accessToken: this.issueStubToken(
      "access",
      username
    )
  };
}

Why the exceptions matter

  • ConflictException → 409 when a username already exists
  • UnauthorizedException → 401 for bad login credentials
  • The same 401 shape is used for an invalid refresh token
  • The controller does not manually assemble status codes

Logout extension

logout(refreshToken) 
logout(refreshToken: string) {
  const entry =
    this.findByRefreshToken(refreshToken);

  if (!entry) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      "invalid or expired refresh token"
    );
  }

  const [, user] = entry;

  user.refreshToken = null;

  return {
    loggedOut: true
  };
}

After logout, trying the same refresh token again should fail because the stored token is now null.

One refresh token per user: the skeleton intentionally stores a single refresh token. A second login overwrites the first session. Supporting multiple active sessions would require storing multiple refresh-token records per user.
Quiz hint

Know why the course proves the request/response contract before adding real hashing and JWT verification. Keeping one variable incomplete at a time makes failures much easier to isolate.

4

Secure DB access and password hashing

This section closes the first major security gap: unsafe database queries and plain-text password storage.

Unsafe SQL

When SQL is assembled with string concatenation, user input becomes part of the SQL program itself.

Unsafe SQL 
function findUserUnsafe(username) {
  const sql =
    `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '${username}'`;

  return db.prepare(sql).all();
}

const maliciousInput = "x' OR '1'='1";

console.log(
  findUserUnsafe(maliciousInput)
);
// every user can come back

Parameterized SQL

A placeholder separates SQL syntax from data. The malicious string remains a value instead of becoming executable query logic.

Parameterized SQL 
function findUserSafe(username) {
  return db
    .prepare(
      "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?"
    )
    .all(username);
}

console.log(
  findUserSafe("x' OR '1'='1")
);
// []
Java comparison: this is the exact reason Java uses PreparedStatement rather than concatenating values into a Statement.

bcrypt.hash()

Registration hashes the password before storage. bcrypt generates a random salt internally and includes the salt information in the stored hash.

register + login with bcrypt 
async register(
  username: string,
  password: string
) {
  const passwordHash =
    await bcrypt.hash(password, SALT_ROUNDS);

  this.users.set(username, {
    passwordHash,
    refreshToken: null
  });

  return {
    username,
    registered: true
  };
}

async login(
  username: string,
  password: string
) {
  const user = this.users.get(username);

  const passwordMatches = user
    ? await bcrypt.compare(
        password,
        user.passwordHash
      )
    : false;

  if (!user || !passwordMatches) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      "invalid username or password"
    );
  }
}

bcrypt.compare()

bcrypt does not decrypt the stored hash. It re-hashes the submitted password with the salt embedded in the stored hash and compares the result.

  • Always await bcrypt.compare(...)
  • Never compare the plain password directly to the hash
  • Never invent a custom password hashing scheme
  • Spring equivalent: BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode() and .matches()
Why two identical passwords produce different hashes: each bcrypt call uses a new random salt. That prevents identical passwords across users from producing identical database values.
Quiz hint

Expect questions about why bcrypt is better than a fast general-purpose hash such as SHA-256 for password storage, and why bcrypt.compare() must be awaited.

5

Labs: turn each concept into a verified behavior

The labs are deliberately staged so students can observe what fails before the fix and what changes after it.

Lab 9: add a second provider/controller pair

Start with the working verification route. Register AttemptsController and AttemptsService, then implement the summary logic.

attempts.service.ts - starter 
import { Injectable } from "@nestjs/common";

const attempts = [
  { username: "dave", outcome: "success" },
  { username: "erin", outcome: "fail" },
  { username: "dave", outcome: "fail" },
  { username: "frank", outcome: "success" },
];

@Injectable()
export class AttemptsService {
  // TODO 1: implement getSummary() to return { successCount, failCount },
  // counted from the attempts array above - identical logic to Module
  // 2/3's counting.
  getSummary() {
    throw new Error("TODO 1: implement getSummary");
  }
}
getSummary() - completed 
getSummary() {
  let successCount = 0;
  let failCount = 0;

  for (const attempt of attempts) {
    if (attempt.outcome === "success") {
      successCount++;
    } else if (attempt.outcome === "fail") {
      failCount++;
    }
  }

  return {
    successCount,
    failCount
  };
}

Lab 9 controller

attempts.controller.ts 
// Given, unchanged - once TODO 1 (attempts.service.ts) and TODO 2
// (app.module.ts) are done, GET /attempts/summary should work.
import { Controller, Get } from "@nestjs/common";
import { AttemptsService } from "./attempts.service";

@Controller("attempts")
export class AttemptsController {
  constructor(private readonly attemptsService: AttemptsService) {}

  @Get("summary")
  summary() {
    return this.attemptsService.getSummary();
  }
}

A missing route before registration is a 404. Once the controller is registered, the request reaches the service and exposes TODO 1 instead.

Lab 10

Add validators to RegisterDto and register the controller/service pair. Verify that bad password length and bad email are both reported.

Lab 11

Add POST /auth/logout. Then prove that the same refresh token can no longer be used after logout.

Lab 12

Replace plain-text storage with bcrypt.hash() and bcrypt.compare() while keeping the external API behavior unchanged.

The progression: wire correctly → validate input → prove the auth contract → harden the internals. That sequence keeps each failure understandable.
From wiring to validation to real password security. By the end of these sections, the NestJS app has a clear dependency graph, runtime request validation, a working auth contract, safe query patterns, and real password hashing. The next natural step is replacing stub token strings with real JWT issuance and verification.
